soste: The Cathedral rises on the Great Mosque (1262)
A convent becomes the main square (1891)
PLAN SUR: THE RIVER IS MOVED (1964-69)
The old riverbed becomes a park (1986)
Oceanogràfic, Palau de les Arts, Àgora (2001-09)

cards.title: Balansiya surrenders
lines: The capitulation is signed on 22 September 1238. Jaume I (James I of Aragon) enters the city on 9 October.
That day is still the Valencian Community holiday.

cards.title: The city empties
lines: Muslims who wish to leave may go south of the Xúquer (Júcar). One estimate says 50,000 do.
Houses are shared out to settlers from Aragon and Catalonia in the Llibre del Repartiment.

cards.title: A new Valencia
lines: Valencia's Jews receive a quarter of their own, walled in 1390.
The city refills with new neighbors, new laws and a new language: Catalan.

cards.title: The Furs of Valencia
lines: The laws proclaimed in 1261 give the kingdom its own legal order inside the Crown of Aragon.
Settlers also farm l'Horta, the irrigated garden watered by the Turia's canals.

cards.title: The Cathedral and the water court
lines: The Great Mosque, made a church in 1238, gives way to the Cathedral.
At its Door of the Apostles, the Tribunal de les Aigües still meets every Thursday to settle irrigation disputes.

cards.title: The Black Death
lines: Plague decimates the population in 1348. Epidemics, wars and riots follow for years.

cards.title: A war, a bigger wall
lines: As the War of the Two Peters with Castile begins, Valencia raises a new wall around a city far larger than the Islamic one.
Only Torres de Serrans and Torres de Quart will survive.

cards.title: The Senyera coronada
lines: Peter IV rewards the city's resistance to Castile with the right to use the royal arms and the crown.
The four red bars on gold now wear a crown. Before 1377 the city used the bars without one.

cards.title: Torres de Serrans
lines: The Serranos Towers, finished in 1398, are the northern gate of the city, beside the Turia.

cards.title: El Micalet
lines: The Cathedral's bell tower, the Miguelete, takes almost fifty years to build, from 1381 to 1429.

cards.title: Torres de Quart
lines: The western gate, built from 1441 to 1460 (Quart Towers), is the other gate that will outlive the walls.

cards.title: La Llotja de la Seda
lines: The Silk Exchange: a trading hall for the silk that made the city rich.
Today it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: The largest city of the Crown
lines: In the 15th century Valencia becomes the most populous city of the Crown of Aragon.
Around 1500, about 45,000 people live behind the walls.

cards.title: The Germania
lines: Craft guilds, armed to protect the city during the plague of 1519, turn against the nobles and the government of Charles V.
Once defeated, the revolt leaves the nobility dependent on royal power.

cards.title: Forced conversions
lines: Charles V orders the Muslim vassals of the kingdom to convert in 1526.

cards.title: Stone bridges over the Turia
lines: By 1607 stone bridges cross the river at Serrans, Mar, Real and Sant Josep, joining the older Trinitat.

cards.title: The Moriscos are expelled
lines: Philip III decrees the expulsion on 9 April 1609. In the Kingdom of Valencia the Moriscos are about a third of the people.
In 1613 the city's exchange bank, the Taula de canvi, goes bankrupt.

cards.title: The Basilica and the Falles
lines: The Basilica of the Mare de Déu dels Desemparats, begun in 1652, stands on the east side of the old forum square.
Each March, during the Falles, falleros bring flowers to the Virgin here on the 17th and 18th.

cards.title: The English ride in
lines: On 24 January 1706 English cavalry under the Earl of Peterborough enter Valencia.
The city sides with Charles of Austria, who promised to respect its laws.

cards.title: The Furs are abolished
lines: After the Bourbon victory at Almansa on 25 April 1707, Philip V repeals the Furs, Valencia's own laws, as punishment.
The Nueva Planta decrees fold the kingdom into the Crown of Castile.

cards.title: A prosperous Bourbon city
lines: From 1758 to 1802 Valencia enjoys a period of affluence under Charles III. Silk is its main industry.
The Palau de Justícia is one of its monuments.

cards.title: The city rises
lines: On 23 May 1808 Valencians rise in arms against the French.
Marshal Moncey's 9,000 men fail twice to take the city, on 26-28 June.

cards.title: Suchet takes Valencia
lines: After a siege that began on 3 November 1811, Marshal Suchet forces General Blake to surrender in January 1812.
Joseph Bonaparte moves his court here that summer. The French leave in July 1813.

cards.title: The walls come down
lines: Demolition of the 1356 wall begins on 20 February 1865.
Only Torres de Serrans and Torres de Quart are left standing.

cards.title: The Citadel goes
lines: The demolition of the old citadel, east of the center, ends after the Glorious Revolution of 1868.

cards.title: Capital of a canton
lines: During the Cantonal rebellion of 1873, Valencia is the capital of the short-lived Valencian Canton.

cards.title: Russafa joins the city
lines: Russafa, Patraix, Benimaclet and Beniferri are annexed.
The city grows past the walls that have just come down.

cards.title: The seaside towns join
lines: El Grau, Cabanyal and Campanar are annexed. The city now reaches the sea.

cards.title: A city of 215,687
lines: The silk industry is gone, but Valencia exports wine and citrus.
The 1900 census counts 215,687 people.

cards.title: The Regional Exhibition
lines: From 22 May to 22 December 1909 a fair shows the progress of Valencian farming and industry.
A concrete bridge is built over the Turia for it. A flood will destroy it in 1957.

cards.title: Capital of the Republic
lines: On 6 November 1936 the Spanish Republican government moves to Valencia.
It stays until 31 October 1937.

cards.title: The war ends
lines: On 30 March 1939 Valencia surrenders and Nationalist troops enter the city.

cards.title: Half a million
lines: The 1950 census counts 503,886 people.
Seven years later the river will flood the city.

cards.title: The Turia floods
lines: On 14 October 1957 the river floods the city. At least 81 people die.
The 1909 Exposition bridge is destroyed.

cards.title: The Plan Sur
lines: A 1961 law approves the Plan Sur: send the Turia around the city in a new channel to the south.

cards.title: A city of immigrants
lines: The economy recovers in the early 1960s and the city grows fast, with workers drawn by major urban projects.

cards.title: The river is moved
lines: On 22 December 1969 the Turia is switched into its new channel, south of the city.
The old riverbed is left dry: almost nine kilometers through the center.

cards.title: Growing fast
lines: The 1970 census counts 648,003 people, almost 30 percent more than in 1960.

cards.title: The Senyera becomes official
lines: After a long dispute over identity, the 1982 Statute of Autonomy makes the Senyera coronada, with a blue stripe at the hoist, the flag of the Valencian Community.
It was the city's own flag before it was the region's.

cards.title: A garden in the riverbed
lines: The first stretches of the Jardí del Túria open in 1986. Ricardo Bofill designs its central stretch.
Today the park covers 136 hectares along almost nine kilometers.

cards.title: Calatrava arrives
lines: The Pont Nou d'Octubre, Santiago Calatrava's first bridge in Valencia, crosses the old riverbed in 1989.

cards.title: Ciutat de les Arts i les Ciències
lines: The City of Arts and Sciences rises at the seaward end of the old riverbed. The Hemisfèric opens in 1998.
The Museu de les Ciències, Palau de les Arts and the Oceanogràfic follow.

cards.title: The America's Cup
lines: Valencia is the first European city to host the America's Cup, in 2007.

cards.title: DANA, 29 October 2024
lines: Flash floods strike the towns south of the city. More than 230 people die in the province of Valencia.
We remember them.

cards.title: Valencia today
lines: 841,558 people live here, in the third-largest city in Spain.
